title: Azure Front Door Pricing: Standard vs Premium (2026)
summary: Azure Front Door pricing comes from usage meters, not the base plan. You can identify charges for data transfer, requests, and security rules.
body_markdown:
## What drives Azure Front Door bill spikes


When the estimate counted the plan fee and skipped the meters, the first meter it skipped was data transfer, which **Front Door bills at two points, not one** .


### Data transfer billed in two places


The team priced one leg and assumed the other was free. Both were billed: Front Door charges for data leaving its edge servers to your visitors, and your origin (the server behind it) can charge again for data leaving it toward Front Door.


According to[Oxbow Research](https://oxbowresearch.com/p/the-egress-tax-how-data-gravity-subsidizes) , Google Cloud **marks egress up 24 times, AWS 18 times** and Azure 17 times. Azure is the lowest of the three.


But 17 times wholesale still means every extra gigabyte of video, images or downloads carries a margin you'll feel, so traffic volume sets the bill more than the plan does.


With those multiples in mind, the two legs add up quickly, and the next charge comes from traffic that never helped the business.


Whether a request came from a customer makes no difference to Front Door, because it bills per request. Scrapers, bots and scanners hitting your site are billed like any visitor.


Doing nothing about them means paying for traffic that earns nothing, and the cost scales with how popular your site is with the wrong crowd.


### Add-ons priced separately


Look for the web application firewall (WAF), which filters malicious requests, and you won't find it in the base price. Its rule sets and its per-request inspection are separate lines.


Then there is Private Link, which keeps traffic between Front Door and your origin off the public internet; it is also its own charge. Each looks small alone, and together they were the second surprise on the invoice.


We reached some caps mid-project: each plan limits how many rules or routes you can configure, and hitting them forced a move to a higher plan, which nobody had priced.


You can model every one of these meters before launch and put an alert on each afterward.


An alert only helps if a person sees it. Activepieces takes an Azure budget alert and posts it to Slack or opens a ticket for the owner; it does the alerting and nothing to Front Door itself.


If a connector your team uses is missing, you generate it with AI and add it privately to your own instance, with no vendor release to wait on.


The catalogue of 750 integrations is counted from the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the MIT-licensed monorepo on GitHub, and roughly 60% of them were contributed by the community, so you're relying on community maintenance for most of these integrations.
